title: Stay healthy!
goals: Talk about your exercise and eating routines with the simple present (Does she eat red meat?).
Say what you are doing these days or this month with the present continuous (I'm studying for an exam).

learn.title: Simple present: habits and routines
learn.html:
Use the simple present for habits, routines, and things that are true all the time. With he / she / it, the verb takes -s (go → goes, do → does, study → studies, have → has).

AffirmativeNegativeQuestion
I walk to work.I don't walk to work.Do you walk to work?
She exercises six days a week.She doesn't exercise on Sundays.Does she exercise every day?
They eat a balanced diet.They don't eat red meat.How often do they go to the gym?
  • With doesn't and does, the verb goes back to the base form, with no -s: Does Brian eat red meat?
  • Frequency words (usually, generally, always, never) go before the verb; once in a while, every other day, and six days a week usually go at the end.
  • Short answers: Yes, I do. / No, she doesn't.

watch.why: With she / he / it, the negative is doesn't.

watch.wrong: Does your brother eats fast food?
watch.right: Does your brother eat fast food?
watch.why: After does, the verb is in the base form, with no -s.

watch.wrong: He go to the gym every day.
watch.right: He goes to the gym every day.
watch.why: With he / she / it, the verb takes -s (go → goes).
The simple present doesn't use be + verb.

learn.title: Present continuous: now and these days
learn.html:
Use the present continuous for what is happening now or these days / this month (something temporary, not a permanent habit). Form: be (am / is / are) + verb-ing.

AffirmativeNegativeQuestion
I'm studying for an exam this month.She isn't eating junk food these days.Are you exercising these days?
He's trying to lose weight.We aren't going to the gym now.What are you doing for your stress?

Comparison:

Simple present (always)Present continuous (now / these days)
I usually walk to work.Today I'm taking the bus.
He doesn't go to the gym.He isn't going to the gym this month.
  • Spelling: run → running, swim → swimming, make → making, lie → lying.
  • Typical signal words: now, right now, today, these days, this week / month.
  • Stative verbs (need, want, like, know, and have meaning to own) almost never take -ing: I need more sleep.

watch.wrong: I studying for an exam this month.
watch.right: I'm studying for an exam this month.
watch.why: The present continuous needs be: I'm studying.

watch.wrong: She is go to the gym these days.
watch.right: She is going to the gym these days.

watch.why: The question form in the continuous uses be, not do.
Need is a stative verb: it is used in the simple present.

learn.title: if and when: what you do and when
learn.html:
If and when connect two ideas: when something happens + what you do. In these habit sentences, use the simple present in both parts (no will).

With whenWith if
I take medicine when I have a cold.I take medicine if I have a cold.
When I have a cold, I drink hot tea.If I get a bad fever, I go to the doctor.
  • when = usual events, “every time”: What do you take when you have a cold?
  • if = rare or less certain events: What do you do if you get the flu?
  • If the if / when clause is at the start, put a comma after it: If I have a cold, I stay in bed.
  • If it is at the end, no comma: I stay in bed if I have a cold.

watch.wrong: If I will get a cold, I drink tea.
watch.right: If I get a cold, I drink tea.
watch.why: After if / when, use the simple present, not will.

watch.wrong: I stay in bed, when I have a fever.
watch.right: I stay in bed when I have a fever.
watch.why: When the if / when clause comes at the end, no comma is written.

watch.wrong: When I have a headache I take an aspirin.
watch.right: When I have a headache, I take an aspirin.
watch.why: When the when clause comes at the start, a comma is written.

watch.wrong: When I have a headache, I am taking an aspirin.
watch.right: When I have a headache, I take an aspirin.
watch.why: For a habit, use the simple present in both parts.

learn.title: Showing surprise and asking for more information
learn.html:
To encourage the other person to keep talking, react with an expression of surprise and then ask a follow-up question.

  • Really? / Oh! / Oh, wow! / Wow! — normal surprise; these work with almost anyone.
  • You're kidding! / No way! / Are you serious? / Oh, my gosh! — strong surprise; better with friends and people you know.
  • How come? / Like what? / What's it about? / What do you do? — follow-up questions.
  • That's too bad. / Oh, no! — when the news is bad (don't react with a joke or a happy surprise).
A says…B responds…
I work out twelve hours a week.You're kidding! What do you do?
I don't like to exercise.Oh, really? How come?
I have a terrible toothache.That's too bad. Do you have a dentist's appointment?

With people you don't know well, use Oh! or Really?; avoid very strong surprise.

reading.title: A year of small changes
reading.intro: Read the text about Valeria and answer.
paragraphs: Last January, my friend Valeria decided to change her habits. She works long hours in an office in Guadalajara, and she was always tired. “I eat fast food almost every day, and I don't sleep enough,” she told me. “Once in a while is OK, but every day is too much.”

Now she is trying to stay in shape. She walks to the office three days a week, and she goes to the gym every other day. On Saturdays she takes a yoga class with her sister. These days she is also learning to cook, so she isn't buying so much junk food. Her favorite new dish is chicken with vegetables.

Valeria has a simple plan for hard days. When she feels stressed, she takes a short break and listens to music for ten minutes. If she gets a headache, she drinks water and rests before she takes any medicine. And if she has trouble sleeping, she doesn't use her phone in bed. She puts it in the kitchen and reads a book.
Is her life perfect now? “No way!” she laughs. “This month I'm studying for an important exam, so I'm sleeping only six hours. But I'm not eating junk food, and that's a good start.”

listening.title: A cold and a karate class
listening.intro: Listen to the conversation between two coworkers. You can repeat it.

lines.text: Hi, Elena. You look tired. Are you OK?
Hi, Mark. Not really. I have a terrible cold, and I'm not sleeping well these days.
Oh, that's too bad. What do you do when you have a cold?
I drink hot tea with honey and I stay in bed. If I feel really awful, I take medicine.
Really? I never take medicine. I gargle salt water when I have a sore throat.
No, it works! And I exercise six days a week, so I don't get sick very often.
Six days a week? Wow! What do you do?
I go running in the morning, and I go to the gym on Saturdays. This month I'm also taking a karate class.
Are you serious? Karate? I only walk to the bus stop!
Come with me on Saturday. Do you want to try?
Maybe when I feel better. Thanks, Mark.
